summary:
Lithuania imposes no LGBT-specific entry, visa or residence screening. A trans visitor may enter and move about the country without facing any question about gender identity at the border.

The country offers no working route to legal gender recognition. Article 5.1 of the Lithuanian Civil Code grants unmarried adults the right to change gender through medical intervention, but no implementing legislation has ever been adopted. The Lithuanian Gay League describes the resulting gap as 18 years of legal limbo; LRT and an earlier LGL report count 17. The two counts refer to the same condition: a statutory right with no procedure behind it.

The courts declined to close that gap twice in 2025. In August the Ukmergė Chamber of the Vilnius Regional District Court suspended a civil case concerning the amendment of civil-status gender documents and referred to the Constitutional Court the question of whether the relevant provisions comply with the Constitution. In September the Constitutional Court declined to examine the request, leaving the absence of legal provisions for changing gender markers and personal identification codes in official documents intact.

The practical consequence for a visitor is that documents are read as issued. A foreign passport or identity document carrying a gender marker inconsistent with the holder's presentation will not be matched against any Lithuanian process of recognition, because no such process exists for residents either. The Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson's 2024 national review records both the absence of a legal framework and the absence of a strategic approach to trans rights in the country.

Protection machinery for gender-based violence is thin. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records a systemic lack of targeted support for LGBTI hate-crime victims. Section 170(3) of the Criminal Code explicitly bans public instigation of violence against LGBT people, and a 2010 preliminary investigation found that 160 of roughly 180 hate-speech instances, most of them online, concerned the LGBT community; perpetrators were usually fined and computers were occasionally confiscated.

Public assembly carries a documented record of police failure. In April 2024 the Seimas Ombudsperson found that police had failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to peaceful assembly, citing an inadequate response to hostile provocators at an LGL assembly, and recommended measures to ensure effective assembly rights. Pride events have been repeatedly obstructed: permission refused in 2007, a court halt in 2010 overturned one day before Baltic Pride proceeded amid heavy policing and violence with 12 protesters arrested, and the 2013 march allowed only after litigation through all judicial instances, ending with 28 arrests. Attendance has since risen to roughly 10,000 at the 2019 Vilnius Pride and around 5,000 in 2023.

Partner recognition exists in partial form. Marriage is limited to opposite-sex couples under Article 38 of the 1992 Constitution and Article 3.12 of the Civil Code. On 17 April 2025 the Constitutional Court ruled that the absence of legal regulation of partnership institutions, including for same-sex couples, contradicts the Constitution and granted same-sex couples the right to register partnerships through the courts until the Seimas adopts a comprehensive law. Since January 2019 the Constitutional Court has required that foreign same-sex spouses be granted residence permits, following the 2018 European Court of Justice ruling in Coman and Others.

Harassment in employment is well documented. Reporting in May 2025 set out trans people's accounts of open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse at work, with experts describing systemic labour-market discrimination.

Official hostility has an explicit legislative history. In 2013 the Seimas considered five separate anti-gay and anti-trans bills, among them a ban on gender reassignment on the stated basis that gender is determined genetically from conception, a same-sex adoption ban, fines of up to €1,800 for organisers of events denigrating constitutional moral values, and legalisation of anti-gay speech; the bills did not pass. The Law on the Protection of Minors passed in 2009 by an 87-6 override of President Adamkus's veto banned information on homosexuality accessible to minors; Amnesty International called it a huge step backwards. On 18 December 2024 the Constitutional Court struck down the anti-LGBT provisions of that law as violating Article 25, freedom of speech, and in January 2023 the ECHR Grand Chamber had ruled that the 2014 ban on a children's book depicting same-sex relationships violated Article 10.
tangentialFactors:
The legislative record shows repeated attempts to write anti-trans provisions into statute. The 2013 package included a prohibition on gender reassignment justified by the assertion that gender is genetically determined at conception. Two further attempts, in 2011 and 2013, sought to criminalise public propagation of homosexual relations with fines of 2,000-10,000 litas; Parliament rejected the first unanimously and the second in 2013.

Expression restrictions targeting minors have been the most durable instrument. The June 2009 amendment to the Law on the Protection of Minors banned propaganda of homosexual, bisexual or polygamous relations for under-18s; the presidential veto was overturned, then on 22 December 2009 the anti-LGBT clauses were replaced with a broader ban on information promoting conceptions of marriage or family other than those in the Constitution. That provision was used to restrict a 2013 Pride advertisement to night-time broadcast with an adult-content logo, and in 2014 the Ministry of Culture age-labelled and then banned the children's book Gintarinė širdis because two stories involved same-sex relationships. Article 39.1 of the Public Information Act, amended on 30 September 2010, briefly barred messages that depicted or promoted a sexual orientation; described as a translation error, it was removed on 16 June 2011 with sexual orientation added as a protected ground.

Decriminalisation dates back to 1993, two years after the end of Soviet occupation; same-sex conduct had been criminal during the interwar period and under Soviet rule. The age of consent was equalised at 14 in 2003 to meet EU accession criteria, then raised to 16 on 2 July 2010 for all couples regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

ILGA-Europe's 2025 review also records LGBTI asylum seekers from Cameroon granted protection after a four-year wait amid dire camp conditions and the conviction of a psychologist for coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts, alongside the prosecution of former MP Gražulis for anti-LGBTI ridicule, which was complicated by his immunity as a Member of the European Parliament.

Media and cultural gatekeeping has operated alongside the law: in 2014 all major television stations refused a pro-tolerance LGBT video clip over fears of breaching the Minors law.
localsOnly:
Residents face documented workplace harm. Reporting in May 2025 detailed open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse experienced by trans people in Lithuanian workplaces, with experts identifying systemic labour-market discrimination.

The Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson published The Situation of Transgender People in Lithuania as the second national review in 2024, following a 2019 edition. It covers the legal framework, document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination, data protection and public attitudes, and records both the absence of a legal framework and the lack of a strategic approach to trans rights.

Registered partnership now runs through the courts. Until the Seimas adopts a comprehensive registered-partnership statute, same-sex couples may register a partnership by applying to a court under the Constitutional Court's 17 April 2025 ruling. A partnership bill had been preliminarily approved 46-17 in May 2017 but remained pending as of 2019, and in May 2021 more than 10,000 people protested against partnership legislation in Vilnius.

Adoption remains closed to same-sex couples because marriage is required. Although single applicants are theoretically eligible, adoption by single gay people is not legally possible in practice; President Gitanas Nauseda stated in September 2021 that he would do his best to block adoption demands from Kaunas Pride organisers. Only 24 same-sex households were declared in the 2011 census.

Assembly conditions have improved in scale but not in policing guarantees: the Seimas Ombudsperson's 2024 recommendation that police secure effective assembly rights followed an assembly where hostile provocateurs met an inadequate police response.
outOfScopeNotes:
Sources differ on the length of the legal gender recognition gap, counting it as 18 years in September 2025 and 17 years in August 2025. The discrepancy is not reconciled in the available material; both describe the same unimplemented Civil Code provision.

No source in the inventory addresses how Lithuanian authorities treat a foreign passport carrying a non-binary or otherwise amended gender marker at the border or in daily document checks. That question remains unresolved here.

Whether any trans person has yet obtained a court-ordered partnership registration under the April 2025 ruling is not sourced, nor is the timeline for the Seimas to enact a registered-partnership statute.

The inventory contains no figures specific to trans people on hate-crime reporting, prosecution outcomes or police complaint procedures; the available hate-speech data dates from 2010 and is not broken down by gender identity.

Healthcare barriers are listed as a heading of the 2024 national review, but the specific findings of that section are not reproduced in the summary document available here.
